## When Should We Use a Regression Line?

A scatterplot may appear to have a linear trend even when:

- the data set is too small, or
- the relationship is too weak.

We need a way to decide whether the observed linear relationship is convincing.

## Ice Cream Sales: Only Three Days

Suppose an ice cream vendor records temperature and gallons sold.

| Temperature | Gallons sold |
|--:|--:|
| 73 | 110 |
| 75 | 97 |
| 77 | 105 |

Three points are not much evidence for a reliable model.

## The First Regression Line

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 700 430" role="img" aria-label="Three ice cream sales observations and a downward regression line">
  <line x1="85" y1="350" x2="650" y2="350" stroke="#222" stroke-width="3"/>
  <line x1="85" y1="350" x2="85" y2="35" stroke="#222" stroke-width="3"/>
  <line x1="120" y1="125" x2="610" y2="250" stroke="#c0392b" stroke-width="5"/>
  <circle cx="250" cy="160" r="10" fill="#1f77b4"/>
  <circle cx="335" cy="245" r="10" fill="#1f77b4"/>
  <circle cx="420" cy="195" r="10" fill="#1f77b4"/>
  <text x="360" y="410" text-anchor="middle" font-size="26">Temperature</text>
  <text x="26" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-size="26" transform="rotate(-90 26 205)">Gallons sold</text>
</svg>
```

The fitted line slopes downward. Does warmer weather really reduce ice cream sales?

## Looking at More Data

| Temperature | 73 | 75 | 77 | 65 | 81 | 90 | 82 | 93 | 86 | 79 |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Gallons | 110 | 97 | 105 | 95 | 135 | 160 | 120 | 175 | 140 | 121 |

The larger data set gives a much clearer picture of the relationship.

```{=html}
  <circle cx="410" cy="235" r="9" fill="#222"/><circle cx="610" cy="45" r="9" fill="#222"/><circle cx="485" cy="170" r="9" fill="#222"/><circle cx="355" cy="230" r="9" fill="#222"/>

```

The first three observations are red. By themselves, they did not show the full pattern.

## Overall Significance Test

The **overall significance test** uses a p-value to test whether the linear relationship is statistically significant.

For simple linear regression:

$$H_0: \beta_1 = 0$$

$$H_a: \beta_1 \ne 0$$

The null hypothesis says that the population regression slope is zero.

## What Does the P-Value Mean?

The p-value measures how unusual our sample evidence would be if there were no linear relationship in the population.

- A **small p-value** is evidence against $H_0$.
- A **large p-value** means the data do not give enough evidence against $H_0$.

The p-value does not measure the strength or accuracy of the model.

## Decision at the 5% Level

If $p < .05$:

::: {.decision}
Reject $H_0$. There is a significant linear relationship.
:::

If $p \ge .05$:

::: {.decision}
Fail to reject $H_0$. There is not enough evidence of a significant linear relationship.
:::

## Can We Use the Regression Equation?

A significant result says there is evidence of a linear relationship.

Before using the equation for prediction, also check:

- the scatterplot and residuals,
- $R^2$ and the standard error,
- whether the prediction is within the observed range, and
- whether the data are relevant to the question.

Significance alone does not guarantee useful predictions.

## Practice

A regression output reports $p = .032$ for the overall significance test.

1. Compare the p-value with $\alpha=.05$.
2. State the decision about $H_0$.
3. State the conclusion in context.

## Practice Answer

Because

$$.032 < .05,$$

we **reject $H_0$**.

There is evidence of a statistically significant linear relationship between the explanatory and response variables.

We would still check model accuracy and assumptions before making predictions.
